summary: CLPS Lunar Browser helps people explore conditions around a potential lunar landing site. NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative delivers science and technology payloads to the Moon through commercial providers. Our independent web prototype lets users choose a mission or lunar coordinate and time, then examine sunlight, Earth visibility, and available measured terrain from orbit or a 1.8 m surface view. It combines JPL NAIF SPICE geometry with Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data to show when terrain may block light or line of sight. A conceptual trip planner links a departure pad and launcher to the selected destination, while a printable dossier records assumptions and source data. The tool makes complex lunar information easier to explore and discuss. It is an educational planning prototype, not a flight-certified landing assessment.
details:
Why it matters

Near the lunar poles, the Sun stays low and local ridges can cast long shadows or obstruct Earth. CLPS payload teams and the public need more than a flat map to understand a site's lighting and line of sight.

What we built

CLPS Lunar Browser connects lunar mission context to an interactive Moon explorer. Users choose a destination and time, inspect Sun and Earth geometry, compare 24-hour visibility windows, and view available local measured terrain from orbit or a 1.8 m eye-level camera. An optional trip planner adds launch context. A printable dossier gathers charts, assumptions, terrain status, data credits, and kernel details.

How it works

The React, TypeScript, CesiumJS, and Three.js interface calls a Python/FastAPI analysis service. JPL NAIF SPICE kernels establish lunar orientation and Sun/Earth positions. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation products and catalogued SLDEM2015 local meshes support terrain horizons and surface scenes where available. LROC and NASA visualization assets provide labeled visual context. The interface identifies when terrain coverage is measured, unavailable, or degraded.

Scope and impact

This is an independent Space Apps education and research prototype inspired by CLPS, not an official NASA service. It helps users ask better questions about polar illumination and communications visibility. Decorative rocks, dust, and atmospheric artwork are illustrative, not measured hazards. Cold-trap reference areas are approximate crater context, not verified permanent-shadow masks or ice detections. The trip planner does not verify vehicle compatibility, landing safety, power, thermal conditions, or a radio link budget. Future work includes validated shadow products and user testing.

Team BRAHMOS: Suhas, Dip, Tap, Rishi, Hemanth, and Kush. Generative AI assisted implementation, tests, drafting, and some conceptual artwork; the team remains responsible for reviewing the scientific claims and final project.
